speeches.Suff:: H Ow fares the King, my Lord? speakes he cheerely? Is the Kings will confirm'd? That will confirme my Daughter Queene. How fares his Highnesse? Are all our numbers full? See them arain'd, I will set forward steright. Ned Homes, speake hast thou brought me meate? And thou hast don't, thou hast betraied me. Goe on, goe on. I kisse thee in requitall of this loue. Ah me! Ned Homes we are vndone, Both thou and I betraide. I doe obey, and onely craue this kindnesse, You would be good vnto my Seruant Homes, Where in releeuing me, hath but performde The duetie of a seruant to his Lord. Hast thou betraide me? yet with such a tongue, so smoothly oilde, slight of my dangers feare, O break my heart, this griefe's too great to beare. God pardon thee, and lay not to thy soule This greeuous •… inne: Farwell. And when thou spendest this ill got golde Remember how thy Maister •… life was solde. Thy Lord that gaue thee Lordships, made thee great, Yet thou betraidst him as he sat at meate. On to my graue, tis time that I were dead, When he that held my heart betraies my head. O Iane! now •… ght but fearethy Tytle & thy state, Thou now must leaue for a small graue. Had I bin contented to a bin great, I had stood, But now my rising, is puld downe with blood. Farwell, point me my house of prayers.
speeches.Nor:: Euen as a dying man, whose life Like to quicke lighting, which is no sooner seene, but is extinct. I, thats the point that we leuel at. But oh, the confirmation of that will, tis all, tis all. Sir Thomas booted and spur'd, whether away so fast? The voice of the whole Land-speakes in my tongue It is concluded your Maiestie must ride, From hence vnto the Tower: there to stay Vntill your Coronation. Honorable friends, and natiue peeres, That haue chosen me to be the leader of these martiall troopes, to march against the sister Of our late dead Soueraigne. Beare witnesse of my much vnwillingnesse, In furthering these attemps, I rather ioy to thinke vpon our ancient victories Against the French and Spaniard, Whose high pride we seueld with the waues of brittish shore Dying the hauen of Brit, with guiltie blood, T •… ll all the Harbor seem'd a sanguine poole: Or we desire these armes, we are now to warre Gainst the perfidious northern enemie, Who trembling at our first shocke voice and sight, Like cowards turn'd their backes with shm •… efull flight But those rich spoiles are past: we are now to goe, Being natiue friends, against a natiue foe. In your hands we leaue the Queene elected, She hath seisure of the Tower, If you'be confident, as you haue sworne Your selues true li •… ge men to her highnesse She no doubt, with royall fauour will remunerate The least of your 〈◊〉 . Farwell My teares into your bosomes f •… ll, With one 〈◊〉 I doe include you all. I, I, sor Gods sake on. Tis more then time my friendes, that we were gone. Excunt Omnes. 〈◊〉 . 〈◊〉 Come they in thunder, we will meete with them? In the loudest language that their ordinance speakes, Ours shall answere theirs. Call me a Herald, and in the market place Proclaime Queene •… ane. The streetes are full, The towne is populous, the people gape for noueltie. Trumpets speake to them, That they may answere with an echoning crie, God saue Queene Iane, God saue her Maiestie. Ha? a bare report of Trumpets! Are the slaues horse, or want they arte to speake? O me! This Towne consi •… s on famous Colledges, Such as know both how, and what, and when to speake, Well, yet wee will proceede, and smother what close enuie hath decreed. Ambrose my Sonne, what newes? Boy, speake the worst, That which soundes deadly est, let me heare that first. Then they reuolt the alegeance from my Daugh ter, and giue it to another: God take them to his mercie, they had neede, Of grace and patience, for they both must bleede, Poore Innocentsoules, they both from guilt are free. Boy, thou saist well, And since the Lords haue all reuolted from me, My selfe will now reuolt against my selfe. Call me a Herald to fill their emptie eares, Assist me Sonne, my good Lord Huntington, Euen in this market Towne proclaime Queene Mary. Amen, I beare a part, I with my tongue, I doe not with my heart, Now they can 〈◊〉 , now they can baule and yell, Base minded slaues, sincke may your soules to hell. A Traitor Arundell? haue I not your hand in my commission? let me peruse it: as I 〈◊〉 tis heere, and by your warrant haue so strict proceeded. Is the limits of my warrant broke answere me. And I obey you: when we parted last My Lord of Arundel, our farwell was 〈◊〉 then our greeting now. Then you cride God speede, Now you come on me ere you say take heede: Then you did owe me your best bloods: nay green'd You could not spend them in my seruice. O then it was a double death to stay behinde, But I am ouertooke and you are kinde, I am, beshrew you else, but I submit, My crime is great, and I must answere it. I am a Herald, and chalenge safetie By the lawe of armes. No kna •… Sir Thomas, I am a true man to my Queene, to whome thou art a Traytor. Stand Traitor stand, or thou shalt nere stand •… ore.
Right, & my Sonne is marryed to your daughter. My Lord, in an euen plaine way, I will Deriue the Crowne vnto your Daughters head. What though the King hath left behinde, Two Sisters, lawfull and immediate heires, To succeed him in his Throane Lyes it not In our powers to contradict it? Haue we not the King and Counsels hands vnto it? Tut, wee stand high in mans opinion, And the worldes broad eye. Will you not subscribe your hand with other of the Lords? Not with me, that in my handes, Surprise the Soueraigntie? Dead! send for Heralds, call me Purseuants, Wher's the King at armes? in euerie market towne Proclaime Queene Iane. Set forward then. The Towre will be a place of ample state, Some lodgings in it, will like dead mens sculs, Remember vs of frailty. wher's Captaine Bret? Kinde Arundell, I bind thee to my loue. Once more farwell. How stands the Treasurer addicted to vs? Wee in our selues are strong. Stay Maister Roose, ere you depart receiue an an swere and reward. In the Soueraigne name of Mary our Queene You •… al vppon the sight hereof, Surcease your armes, discharge your Souldiers, And presently repaire vnto the Court, Or else to be held as an Arch-Ttaitor. O maister Roose, it cannot bee, I will assure you At my departure thence, I left liuing there at least Fiue hundred friendes, and now I haue not one, simply not one: friendes! ha, ha, ha, Commission Thou must be my friend. And stand betiwixt me and the stroake of death, Were thy date out, my liues date were but short, They are colde friends, that kils their friends in sport My 〈◊〉 friend! O my Children! my soule weepes endlesse teares for you. O at the generall Sessions, when all soules Stand at the bar of Iustice, And hold vp their new immortalized handes, O then lot the 〈◊〉 of their tragick endes Be racd out of the bed-rowle of my sinnes: When ere the black booke of my crime's vnclaspt. Let not these scarlet Letters be found there: Of all the rest, onely that page be cleere. But come to my arraignement, then to death, The Queene and you haue long aim'd at this head, If to my Children, she sweet grace extend, My soule hath peace, and I imbrace my end. Exeunt.
Heere comes Sir Thomas Wyat. Best to take the opinion of the Counsell. Why sighes your Maiestie? Neuer, and it like your grace. Three daies are past, Monday, Tuesday and Wed nesday too Yet my protesting seruant is not come. Himselfe conducted me to this hard lodging, A simple Cabin, for so great a Prince, And then he swore, but oathes you see are vain •… , That he would hourely come and visite me: I that was wont, to sur 〈◊〉 in estate, Am now through hunger almost desolate. I prethee doe, neede bids me eate, Neede bids me heare thee too.
It bootes me not to stay, When in this land rebellion beares such sway. Gods will, a Court! Tis chang'd Since Noble Henries daies. You haue set your handes vnto a will. A will you well may call it: So wils Northumberland: So wils great Suffolke, Against Gods will, to wrong those Princely Maides. Health to the Lady Mary. In actions roauing •… rom the bent of truth, We haue no persident thus to persist But the bare name of worldly policie. If others haue ground from Iustice, and the law, As well diuine as politicke agreeing, They are for no cause to be disinherited. If you not seauen yeares since •… o that effect, Swore to the Father to maintaine his seede, What dispensation hath acquited you From your first sacred vowes? Youle say, the will extorted from a childe. O! let m •… ne eyes in naming that sweete youth, Obserue their part, Powring downe teares, sent from my swelling heart. God, mother, I tearme childe? but ile goe on, Say that the will were his, forced by no tricke, But for religions loue his simple act, Yet note how much you erre. You were sworne before to a mans will, and not a will alone, But strengthned by an act of Parliament. Besides this sacred proofe. The Princely Maides, Had they no will nor act to prooue their right? Haue birthrights no pri •… ledge, being a plea so strong, as cannot be refeld, but by plaine wrong? Now were you toucht. The Lady in tower, alasse shee's innocent of my claime. Trust me, shee'd thinks •… t a moste happy life, To leaue a Queenes, and keepe a Ladies name. And for the Dukes, your warrants sent them foorth, Let the same warrant call them backe againe. If they refuse to come, the Realme, not they Must be regarded. Be strong and bold: We are the peoples factors. Saue our Sonnes From killing one another, be affraide, To tempt both heanen and earth, so I haue said. Neuer make doubt, setting her ceremonious or der by. She is pure within, and mildly chast without. What neede hee (Noble Lords) to aske the fruite, when he demaundes the tree? No Castle, 〈◊〉 , nor Towers of strength, It bootes not, when the chiefest Tower of all The key that opens vnto all the Land. I meane our Gratious Soueraigne must be his, But he will beare no office in the land, And yet will marry with the Queen •… of all. Nor be of counsell in the Realmes affaires, And yet the Queene inclosed in his armes: I doe not like this strange marriage The Fox is suttle, and his head once 〈◊〉 The slender body easily will follow. I grant, he offers you in name of dowre, The yearely summe of threescore thousand Duc cats. Besides, the seauenteene famous Prouinces, And that the heire suceeding from your loynes, Shall haue the Souereigne rule of both the R •… almes. What, shall this mooue your Highnesse to the match? Spaine is too farre for England to inherit, But England neare enough for Spaine to woe. Which of you all, dares iustifie this match, And not be toucht in conscience with an oath? Remember, O remember I beseech you, King Henries last will, and his act at Court, I meane that royall Court of Parliament, That does prohibit Spaniards from the Land, That Will and Act, to which you all are sworne, And doe not damme your soules with periurie. Hee that loues freedome and his Countrie, Crie a Wyat: he that will not, with my heart Let him stand foorth, shake handes, And weele depart. Knocke him downe, fie no, Weele handle him, he shall sound before he goe. Sweete musicke, Gallant fellow-Londi ners. You shall be all Lord Maiores at least, Those eight 〈◊◊〉 shall doe seruice now against their Maisters Norfolke and Arundell, They may t •… their heeles more then their hands for sauing of their liues, When souldiers turne surueyors and measure Lands, God helpe poore 〈◊〉 . Souldiers and friend •… , let v •… all play ni •… ble bloud, Houndes, and hunt them step by step, We heare the Lawyers plead in Armour steede of Gownes, if they fall out about the case they Iar, Then they may c •… each 〈◊◊◊〉 the Bar. Soft, this is Ludg are, stand 〈◊◊〉 knock. A Wyat, a true friend, Open your gates, you louring Citizen •… , I bring you freedome, from a 〈◊〉 Prince, The Qu •… has heard your suite, And tis her pleasure the C •… tie gates, Stand open to 〈◊〉 vs. She commaundes hy vs. O London, London, thou perfidious Town, Why hast thou broke, thy promise to thy friend? That for thy sake, and for thy generall sake, Hath thrust my selfe into the mouth of danger? March backe to Fleet-streete, if that Wy •… t die, London vniustlie, buy thy treacherie. Traitor and Wyats name, Differ as farre as Winchester and ho •… .
Ile damb'd my soule for no man, no for no man, who at doomes day must answere for my sinne: Not you, nor you my Lordes, Who nam'de Queene Iane in noble Henries daies, Which of you all durst once displace his issue? My Lords, my Lords, you whet your kniues so sharp, To carue your meate, That they will cut your fingars. The strength is weakenesse that you builde vpon, The King is sicke, God mend him, I, God mend him: But were his soule from his pale body free, Adieu my Lords, the Court no court for me. Thats my name indeede.
Farwell, I feare thee not. The Fly is angrie, but hee wants a sting, And all the Counsell: onely this peruerse And peeuish Lord, hath onely deny'd his hand To the inuesting of your princely Daughter. Hee's idle, and wants power. Our Ocean shall these petty brookes deuoure, Heere comes his Highnesse Doctor.
speeches.Doct:: His body is past helpe. We haue left our practice to the Diuines, That they may cure his soule
speeches.Aru:: Past phisickes helpe, why then past hope of life, Heere comes his Highnesse Preacher: Life reuerent man. Your sacred Highnesse will no doubt be minde full of the late Oath you tooke at 〈◊◊〉
Life, life, though death his body doe disseuer, Our King liues with the King of heauen for euer.
You are too timorous. We in our selues Are power sufficient: the King being dead. This hand shall place the crowne On Queene Ianes head. Trumpets and Drums, with your notes resound, Her royal name, that must in state be crown'd. Exeu ̄ t Om
speeches.Guil:: Our Cousen King is dead. Intreate not Iane, though shee our bodies part, Our soules shall meete. Farwell my loue. 〈1 line〉 And would to God, this 〈◊◊◊◊◊〉 , Might haue 〈◊◊◊◊◊◊〉 , For 〈◊◊〉 , and 〈◊◊◊〉 weale. Dooe's Trees want sence, that by the power of musick? haue bene drawn to dance a pleasing mea sure, w •… come then 〈◊〉 vnto liuing thinges, say wee vsurpe the English Royaltie, wast not by your I tel you Lords, I haue your hands to show, Subscrib'd to the Commission of my father, cons •… ? By which, you did authorice him to wage armes, If they were Rebellious against your Sou •… aigne Who cride so loude as you, God saue Queene Iane? And come you now your Soueraigne to arraigne? Come downe, come downe, here at a Prisoners barre Better doe so, then iudge your selues amisse •… For looke what 〈◊〉 , on our heads you lay, Vpon your owne, may light another day. And wee must die, for a lesse fault, O partiallitie! VVhy this is well, since we must die, That wee must die together. Good morrowe once more to my lo •… lye Iane. VVhat were you reading? Trust me so was I, wee hade neede to pray, For see, the Ministers of death drawe neere. My Lord High Chancelor, you are wel come heather, What come you to beholde our execution? And my Lord Arundell, thrice welcome, You helpt to attache our Father, come you now, To see the blacke conclusion of our Tragedie? So doe wee. Our office is to die, yours to looke on: VVe are beholding vnto such beholders, The time was Lords, when you did flock amaine, To see her crownd, but now to kill my Iane, The world like to a sickell, bends it selfe, Men runne their course of liues as in a maze, Our office is to die, yours but to gaze. And demaundes a pardon, Onely of her, for taking off her head? But ile not pardon him, thou art my wife. And he shall aske me pardon for thy life, Oh!
speeches.Ian:: Alasse, how small an Vrne containes a King? He that ruld all, euen with his princely b •… eath, Is forc'd to stoope now to the stroake of death. Heard you not the proclamation? To whome my Lord bends this your aue. O God! me thinkes you sing my death, In parts of musickes lowdnes, Tis not my turne to rise. O God! My Lord and Father, I pray tell me, Was your Fathers Father ere a King?
speeches.Gui:: I heare of it, and I giue credit to it What great men feare to be, Their feares grow greater. Our Fathers grow ambitious And would force vs saile in mightie tempests, And are not Lordes of what they doe possesse. Are not thy thoughts as great? Euen what you will, Yet saue my Iane, although my blood you spill. Norfolk •… no, I speake to — Alasse I doe not knowe whi •… h of 〈◊〉 dies first. 〈◊◊◊◊◊〉 Rise, doe not kneele. Th •… ugh thou submit'st, thou hast a lowring steele Whose fatal declynation brings our death: Good man of earth, make haste to make vs ear •… . O doe not kill me with that 〈◊〉
I haue no thoughts so ranke, so growne to head, As are our Fathers pride. Troth I doe inioy a Kingdome hauing thee. And so my paine be prosperous in that, What care I though a Sheep-cote be my Pallace Or fairest roofe of honour. Would I might still continue of his lyne, Not trauell in the cloudes. It is often seene, the heated blood That couets to be royall, leaues off ere it be noble, My learned carefull King, what must we goe? Then it must be so.
See how thy blood keepes course with mine: Thou must be a Queene, aye me! a Queene, The flattering belles that shrilly sound At the Kings funerall with hollow heartes, Will cowardly call thee Soueraigne: For indeed thou wouldst prooue but an Vsurper. We must. We are led with pompe to prison, O propheticke soule. Lo we ascend into our chaires of State, Like funerall Coffins, in some funerall Pompe descending to their graues. But we must on. How can we fare well, to keep our Court: Where Prisoners keepe their caue? I pra'y resolue vs good Maister Lieftenant Who was it yonder, that rendered vp his life To natures death? True, my faire Queene of sorrowe truely speake. Great men like great Flies, Through lawes Cobw •… breake, But the thin'st 〈◊〉 the prison of the weake. O I shall faint againel Yet let me beare this fight vnto my 〈◊〉 My sweete Ianes head: Looke Norfolke, Arundell, Winches •… Doe male factors, looke: Thus when they die 〈◊〉 ruddi •… lippe, A cleere reflecting eye, Cheekes purer then the Maiden oreant 〈◊〉 That 〈◊〉 bash •… lnes through the 〈◊〉 Her innocence, has giuen her this looke: The like for me to show so well being dead, How innocence, would Guilford loose his head.
speeches.Ian,: Who would weare fetters though they were all of golde? Or to be sicke, though his faint browes For a wearing Night-cap, wore a Crowne. Thou must assume, a tytle that goes on many feet, But tis an office, wherein the heartes of Schollers, And of Souldiers will depend vppon thy Hearse. Were this rightly scand, Wee scarce should finde a King in any Land.
Honor and happy reigne Attend the new Maiestie of England. To your grace dread Soueraigne, You are by the Kings will, and the consent Of all the Lords, chosen for our Queene. Heauens giue your grace successe. Commend vs to the Queene and to your Sonne, Within one weeke, I hope war will be done. Speake like a Gentleman, vpon your word Are you not disc •… ntent? You haue said nobly, sit and take your place. It may be that it hath pleased her Maiestie To pardon vs, and for to punnish you. I know no other reason, this I must, I am commounded, and the act is Iust. What is your Highnesse pleasure about the Rebels? Count Edmond the Embassador from Spaine, attends your highnesse answere, brought those Letters sent from the Emperor In his Sonnes behalfe. I say and it like your royall Maiestie, a royall treatie, and to be confirm'd, and I alowe the match. Wiat is march •… downe Fleete-streete: after him.
Thus like a Nun, not like a Princesse borne, Descended from the Royall Henries loynes: Liue I inuirond in a house of stone, My Brother Edward liues in pompe and state, I in a mansion here all ruinate. Their rich attire, delicious banquetting: Their seuerall pleasures: all their pride and honour, I haue forsaken for a rich prayer Booke. The Golden Mines of wealthy India, Is all as drosse compared to thy sweetnesse. Thou art the ioy, and comfort of the poore, The euerlasting blisse in thee we finde. This little volume inclosed in this hand, Is richer then the Empire of this land. By Gods asistance, and the power of heauen, after our Troubles we are safely set, In our inheritance, for which we doe subscribe The praise and benefit to God, next thankes To you my Lordes. Now shall the sanctuarie, And the house of the moste high be newly built. The ancient honours due vnto the Church, Buried within the Ruine Monastaries, Shall lift their stately heads, and rise againe To astonish the destroyers wandring eyes. Zeale shall be deckt in golde, Religion not like a virgin robd of all her ponipe, But briefly shining in her Iemmes of state, Like a faire bride be offerd to the Lord. To build large houses pull no churches downe, Rather in rich the Temple with our crowne. Better a poore Queene, then the Subiects poore. But that wee knowe thee Wyat to be true Vnto the Crowne of England and to vs, Thy ouer-boldnesse should bee payde with death. But cease, for feare your liberàll tongue of fend, With one consent my Lordes you like this match? Call in Count Edmond Honorable Lords. Wee haue determined of your Ambassie, and thus I plight, our loue to Philips heart, Imbarke you straight, the winde blowes wondrous faire: Till he shall land in England, I am all care.
Pardon me Madam, that so boldly I presse into your Chamber. I salute your Highnesse with the high stile of Queene.
Queene! may it be? Or iest you at my lowring miserie. I see my God, at length hath heard my prayer. You Sir Harry, for your glad tydings, Shall be held in honour and due regard. And why not Queene, Sir Thomas? The Queene-like Rebels, Meane you not Queene Iane? Wiat no more, the law shall be their Iudge, Mercie to meane offenders weele ostend, Not vnto such that dares vsurpe our Crowne.
speeches.Ben:: Your Brother King is dead, And you the catholicke Queene must now succede.
speeches.Wia:: Aske that of Suffolke duke, & great Northumber land Who in your steede hath Crown'd another. Nothing more true then that: Nothing more true then you are the true heire, Come leaue this Cloyster and be seene abroad, Your verie sight will stirre the peoples heatts, and make them cheerely, for Queene Maries crie. One comfort I can tell you: the tenants of the Dukes Northumberland and Suffolke denide their ayde, In these vnlawfull armes: to all the Counsell I denide my hand, and for King Henries Issue still will stand. Come let vs streight from hence, From Framingham: Cheere your spirits. Ile to the Dukes at Cambridge, and discharge them all: Prosper me God in these affaires, I lou'd the Father wel, I lou'd the Sonne, And for the Daughter I through death will run. Exeunt Omnes. I had forgot: when we weare at counsell, He stole away, and went home to his house, And by much intreatie was woon to returne, In briefe they all incline to Queene Mary My Lord farwell, each hastic houre: Will coulder tydings cell. The Lady Iane most mightie Soueraigne, Alyde to you in blood: for shes the Daughter of your Fathers Sister. Mary the Queene of France: Charles Brandons Wife your Neece, your next of blood, except your sister, Deserues some pittie, so doth youthfull Guilford. And you to proude vouchsafe? O base! I hope sheele no •… vouchsafe to take the Emperors sonne to her deare mercie. What loude knaues that? Stay, lets know him first. Wheres all my Souldier •… ? what all gone, And left my Drum and colours without guard? O infilicitie of carefull men! Yet will I sell my ho •… oured blood as deere, •… s euer did faithfull subiect to his Prince.
speeches.Mar:: another Queene, Sir Thomas wee aliue, The true immediate heires of our dread Father? In the behalfe of louely Princely Philip, Whose person wee haue shrined in our heart? at the first sight of his delightfull picture That picture should haue power to tingle Loue in Royall brests: the Dartes of loue are wordes, pic tures, conceite, heele preuaile by any, Your counsell Lords about this forraine businesse.
speeches.Mary:: Your Counsel, good sir Thomas, is so pithy That I am woon so like it.
speeches.Bre:: Heere my Lord. They are my Lord. Why the Souldiers? I say again •… , is worthy Norfolke gone? I say agen, th •… t Wyat 〈◊〉 thus, In 〈◊〉 with the 〈◊◊〉 thus at his taile, is worthy to be hang'd like a 〈◊〉 in the King domes 〈◊〉 , say I well my Lads? And wherefore is Wyat vp? Philip is a Spaniard, and what is a Spani ard? Right, a Spaniard is a Camocho, a Calliman co, nay which 〈◊〉 worse, a Dondego, and what is a Dondego? Tis the Lord Pembroke. What should wee doe following Wyat anye longer. Wold I could steale away from Wyat, it should be the first thing that I would doe,
speeches.A •… :: My Lord most lou'd with what a mourning heart I take your farwell, let the after signes Of my imploym nt witnesse. I protest. Did not the sacred person of my Queene, Whose weale I tender as my soules cheefe blisse, Vrge my abode, I would not thinke it shame To traile a pike where you were generall. But wishes are in vaine, I am bound to stay, And vrgent businesse calls your grace away. See, on my knees I humbly take my leaue, And steep my wordes with teares. I helpt to attach the Father, but the sonne — O through my blood, I feele compassion. Ru •… my Lords, weele be humble suters to the Queen to saue these innocent creatures from their deathes.
Come my Lords, shall vs march. Sir I meane quarter them, that the offended multi tude, may passe in safetie. Not in any sorte the Dukes pleasure will pasle free. Sir •… , this is a famous Vniuersitie, and those schol lers, those lofty buildings and goodly houses, Founded by noble Patrons. But no more. Set a strong watch. That be your 〈◊〉 care. Tis good, tis good, my Lord. No, a Dondego is a desperate Viliago, a very Castilian, God blesse vs. There came but one Dundego into England, & hee made all Paules stincke agen, what shall a whole a •… my of Dondegoes doemy sweete Countrimen?
speeches.Tre:: What ho Porter! open the gate. Then will I flie this fearefull Counsell boord, Ex it Tre.
I beseech your honour to pardon me, The Couns •… hath giuen 〈◊〉 commaund Not 〈◊〉 shall 〈◊〉 this way. Well my Lord, I doe aduenture on your word. The Dukes displeasure: all the Counsell boord Bésides, may be my heauie enemies, But goe a Gods name, I the worst will proue, And if I die, I die for him I loue. My Lords, Sir Thomas Wyat craues accesse vnto your honours. Roume for Sir Thomas Wyat.
Why you idle fellow, am I not sent vppon the Queenes affaires, commanded by the Lords? and know you not that I am Treasurer? come open the Gate, 〈◊〉 doe you know not what. I thanke thee, and will warrant thee from death. Is my Horse ready? My Lord, the businesse of these troublous times, Binding vs al, still to respect the good of common weale: Yet doth it not debar priuate regard of vs & of our own The generall weale is treasur'd in your brest, And all my ablest powers haue bin imployed To stir them there, yet haue I borne a part, Laying the commons troubles next my heart, My ouersight in parting without leaue: Was no contempt, but onely for an houre. To order home affaires, that none of mine, In these nice times should vnto faction clime. Troth to be plaine, I am not pleas'd, That two such princely Maides lineally descended, From our royall King, and by his testimonie, Confirmed heyre, if that their Brother dying Issules, And one that neuer dream't, it neuer desired The rule of Soueraignetie, But with virgins teares hath oft bewaild her miserie, Should politickly by vs be nam'd a Queene.
speeches.Por:: It is my Lord My heart misgiues me, I haue done amisse, Yet being a Counsellor one of the number Nothing can prooue amisse. Now shall I know the worst. Heere comes my Lord of Arundell. But now my gratious Lord.
speeches.Arun:: Porter, Did the Lord Treasurer passe this way? Vngratious Villaine, follow, Bring him backe againe, If not, by faire meanes bring him backe by force: And heare you sirra, as you goe, will the Lord Maior and some Aldermen of his Bretheren, and some espe ciall Citttzens of note, to attend our further pleasures presently. 〈◊〉 Treasurer fled: the Duke is but newly ar rested, some purpose, on my life, to crosse their plots: weeleset strong watches, see Gates and walles well mand: tis ten to one but princely innocence, Is these strange 〈◊〉 wisest violence. Though' your attempt, Lord Treasurer be such, That hath no colour in these troublous times, But an apparant purpose of reuolt, From the deceast Kings will, and our degree, Yet, for you are a Counsellor of note, One of our number, and of high degree, Before we any way presume to iudge, We giue you leaue to speake in your behalfe. A rise sir Thomas, sit and take your place. Now to our former businesse: The obligation wherein we all stood bound To the deceased late Kings will and our decree, His cousen Iane, and the two absent Dukes Cannot be conceal'd without great reproach To vs and to our Issue. We haue sworn in presence of the sacred host of heauen Vnto our late young Lord, to both the Dukes, That no impeachment should diuert our heartes From the impeachment of the Lady Iane. To this end we haue ceased her in the tower, By publike proclamation made her Queene: To this end we haue armed the Duke, with power Giuen them commission vnder our owne handes To passe against the Lady. You performe in hostile ma ner And no doubt, the spleene of the vndanted spirit Of Northumbers Earle, will not be called With writings of repeale. Aduice in this, I holde it better farre To keepe the course we runne then seeking chan •… , Hazard our liues, our heires and the Realmes. Why then giue order that she shall be Queene, Send for the Maior, her errors wele forget, Hoping she will forgiue. Giue order to keepe fast the Lady Iane, Dissolue the the Counsell. Let vs leaue the Tower, and in the Citie hold our audience. I am no friend to Traitors: in my moste high & Princely Soueraignes name, I doe ar •… st your honour of high Treason. Guilford and Iane, with great Northumberland, and hauty Suffolkes Duke. Pray pardon me, doe what you will to day, And ile approue it though it be my death. Hee's fal •… into a 〈◊〉 .
Nay my good Lord, be plaine with vs, I pray, Are you not grieu'd that we haue giuen consent To Lady Ianes election?
speeches.Arun: Let him come neare. You must with your three Sons, be guarded safe Vnto the Tower: with you, those Lords and Knights That in this faction did associate you, For so I am inioyn'd. Then peaciuely, let 〈◊〉 conduct you thither,
A diuine spirit teach your honours truth, Open your eyes of iudgement to beholde The true Legitimate, Mary your vndoubted soueraigne. You haue aduised well honorable Lordes, So will the Citizens be wholly ours, and if the Dukes be crosse, weele crosse their powers.
speeches.Clo:: What shall we quarter Captaine? The Co ̄ mons shal be vsed with al co ̄ mon curtesie That goes in rank like beanes and chees •… -cakes on their heads in steade of Cappes. Crie 〈◊〉 saue the Queene as you goe, and God send you a good market. O poore shrimpe, how art thou falne away for want of mouching? O Colen cries out most tirannically, the little gut hath no mercie, whats heere vittailes? O rare! O good! Feede chops, drinke throate, good vict ailes makes good blood. But stay, whose heere? more Sheriffes more searchers? O no, this is Homes that betraide his honest Maister, How, with a Halter about his necke? I hope hee doth not meane to hang himselfe? ile step a side. This is rare, now in this moode hee would hang himselfe tw •… re excellent. So, so, a very good ending, would all falce Seruants might drinke of the same sauce. Gold, you are firstmine, you must helpe To shift my selfe into some counterfeite suite Of apparel, and then to London: If my olde Maister be hanged, why so: If not, why rusticke and lusticke: Yet before I goe, I doe not care if I throwe this Dog in a Ditch: come away dissembler: this cannot chuse but be a hundred pound it wayes so heauy. Because he cannot keep •… his 〈◊〉 . A Spaniard is no Englishman that I knowe. A Dondego is a kinde of Spanish Stockfish, or poore Iohn. Marry they will make vs all smell abhomi nably, hee comes not heere that's flat. That's the reason our Englishwomen loue them not. Weele fling our flat Caps at them. Kill him, then le •… know him afterwards.
Why they are not hang'd nor drawn'e yet? May we not take tooles of the pie •… & the aple-wo men What carry you there in your basket? Mat. Egs •… or sooth.
Feare not, good speech, thuse rude armes I beare, Ist n •… t to fight, Sweet, gentle Peace away, But to succour your liues, passe peaceibly away.
speeches.〈◊〉 . [Countryman]: God saue the Queene, what Queene? there lies the se •… se When we haue none, it can be no offence.
Well, crie God saue Queene Iane as you goe, and God s •… nd you a good Market.
Is the right Queene called Iane? alacke for woe, at the first she was not christened so. 〈◊〉 my Lord of Winchester I pra'y.
Thus olde and young still descant on her name, Nor lend no eare, when wee horstile proclaime. I feare, I feare. Fear Bret, what shouldst thou feare? Thou hast a brest compos'd of adamant. Fa •… l what ill betide, my anchor is cast, and I in Harbor ride. Heere my Lord. I am to lead you, & whether? to fight: and with whome? with Wyat: and what is Wyat? a moste fa mous and Arch-Traytor, to nobody by this hand that I knowe.
My Lord tis true, you sent vnto the Counsell for fresh supplies, what succour, what supplies? Happie is he can draw his necke out of the coller, and make his peace with Marie. My Lord of Winchester, still thirsts for 〈◊〉 . Vouchsafe! my Lord of Winchester, pray what? To marrie with our Queene: mean •… you not so? I graunt, your predecessors oft haue sought Their Qu •… ne from France, And sometimes to from Spaine. But neuer could I heare that England yet Has bin so base, to seeke a King from either: Tis policie deare Queene, no loue at all. And ere hee land in England, I will offer My loyall brest for him to treade vpon. O who so forward Wyat as thy selfe, To raise this troublesome Queene in this her Throane? Philip is a Spaniard, a proud Nation, Whome naturally our Countrie men abhorre. Assist me gratious heauens, and you shall see What hate I beare vnto their Slauerie. Ile into Kent, there muster vp my friendes, To saue this Countrie, and this Realme defend. Sir George be ruld, Since we professe the Arte of Warre, Let's not be hist at for our ignorance, Hee shall passe and repasse, iuggle the best he can, Lead him into the Crai •… . Norry set foorth Set foorth thy brasen throate and call all Rochester About thee: doe thy office, fill their Light heads with proclamations, doe, Catch Fooles with Lime-twigs dipt with pardons. But Sir George and good sir Harry Isley, If this Gallant open his mouth too wide, Powder the Varlet, pistoll him, fire the Roofe that's ore his mouth He craues the law of Armes, and he shall ha't, Teach him our law, to cut's throate if he prate. If lowder reach thy Proclamation, The Lord haue mercie vppon thee. A March! 〈◊〉 Norfolkes Drum vpon my life. I pra'y see what Drum it is. The word is giuen, arme, arme flies through the camp As loude, though not so full of dread 〈◊〉 thunder: For no mans 〈◊〉 looke pale, but euerie face, Is lifted vp aboue his foremans head, And euerie Souldier does on 〈◊〉 stand, shaking a drawne sword in his threatning hand. Lords I yeeld, an easie conquest tis to win the field, After al's lost I am wounded, let me haue a surgion, that I may goe 〈◊〉 vnto my grau •… . Tis not the name of Traitor paules me, Nor pluckes my weapon from my hand. Vse me how you can, though you say Traitor, I am a Gentleman. Your dreadfull shaking me, which I defie, Is a poore losse of life, I wish to die, Death 〈◊◊〉 spirit, no more then can my bed, Nor will I change one haire, loosing this head.
O my thrice honoured Father, The Lords haue all re uolted from your faction
speeches.Am:: In Baynards Castle was a counsell held, Whether the Maior and Sheriffes did resort, And twas concluded to proclaime Queene Mary. True my thrice honoured Father, Besides, my brother Guilford and his wife Where she was proclaimde Queene, are now close Prisoners, namely in the Tower.
O my thrice honoured Father! might I aduise you, flie to your manner, there studdie for your saftie. Heere come •… s your honoured friend the Earle of Arundell.
Mary by the grace of God, Queene of England, France and Ireland, defendres of the Faith. Amen.
speeches.〈◊〉 : [Roose]: My honored Lord, the Counsell greetes you with these Letters.
Tis short & sharp, Maister Roose, we do obey your warrant: but I pray tel mee, how doth all our friendes at Court? is there not a great mortalitie amongst them? Is there not a number of them deade of late since I came thence?
speeches.Hom:: With much a doe my Lord, meat, bread & wine, While you refresh your selfe, I will recorde The cause of my long stay. And I no sooner entred but attached, Threatned the Rack: and if I did not yeeld Your gracious selfe into their gracelesse hands. and offer'd a thousand Crownes to him that can Bring newes of your abode, twas offer'd in my hands. Which I beseech may stop my Vitall breath, When I am feede with golde to worke your death. and in requitall of so great a grace, I kisse your hand that dares to kisse my face.
The night I left you in the hollow tree, My house was searched. Done it! o betraie you? O noe! First would I see my loued wife and Children Murdered, and tos'd on speares, before I would Deliuer your grace vnto their handes, For they intend your death. O God, O God, that euer I was borne, This deede hath made me (slaue) to abiect scorne.
speeches.She:: So Iudas kist his Maister: ceaze the Duke.
My Lord, late Duke of Suffolke, in her highnesse name I doe arrest you of high Treason. You are deceiu'd sir in your seruant much, Hee is the man that did betray you. Heere Maister Homes, towards your thousand pounds, Heere is a hundred markes, Come to the Exchequer, you shall haue the rest.
speeches.Ho:: Pardon me my Lord. Shall I aske mercie? no it is too late, Heauen will not heare, and I am desperate.
This is the place, where I betraide my Lord, This is the place where oft I haue releeu'd: and villaine I, betraide him to the Iawes of death, But heere before I further will proceede Heere will I burie this inticing gould, Lye there damn'd fiend neuer serue humaine more,
May it please your grace to giue release Vnto such ancient Bishops that haue lost their Honours in the church affaires. Such pittie as the law alowes to Traitors. What Sonne to obey his Father proues a Traitor, Must buy their disobedience with their death. Alow it Lordes, we haue cause To thanke our God, that such a mightie Prince as Phillip is, Sonne to the Emperor, Heire to wealthy Spaine, and many spacious Kingdomes, will vouchsase — To grace our mightie Soueraigne with his honourable Title. I doe, what then? W •… at you are too hot. Then 〈◊〉 I say, we haue cause to thanke our God, That such a mightie Prince will look •… so lowe, As to respect this Iland and our Queene. Has not the Kinges of England (good Sir Thomas) Espous'd the Daughters of our Neighbour Kinges? Tis loue great Queene, no pollicie at all. My Lord of Norfolke, will it please you sit By you the noble Lord of Arundell, Since it hath pleasde her sacred Maiestie, To nominate vs heere Commissioners: Let vs without all partialitie be open eard, To what they can 〈◊〉 : where's the Lieftenant of the Tower? O my Lord of Arundell, wee remember that, But shall a Subiect force his Prince to sweare Contrarie to her conscience and the Law? Wee heere release vnto our faithfull people, one 〈◊〉 Subsidie, Due vnto the Crowne in our dead Brothers daies. The Commonaltie shal not be 〈◊〉 burdned In our reigne, let them be liber all in Religion, and wee will spare their treasure to themselues: Better a poore Prince then the Nation poore, The Subiects Treasure, in the Soueraignes store.
speeches.Ma:: The Duke of Suffolke is not yet apprehended, Therefore my Lords, Some of you most deare to vs in loue, Be carefull of that charge: The rest weele leaue for try all of the other prisoners.
They were misled by their ambitious Fathers, Yonder the Traitor marcheth with a ste •… le bowe. Bent on his Souereigne, and his kingdomes peace: To waue him to vs with a flag of truce, And tender him soft mercie, Were to call our right in question, Therefore put in act, your resolute intendments, If rebellion be suffered to take head, She liues too long, treason doth swar •… e. Therefore giue signall to the fight, Where's Captaine Bret? And there being mist, some villaine finding you out of sight hath raisde this slander on you, but come my Lord. Come leaue your swearing, Did not countries care vrge me to this quarrell? For my part I would not strike a blowe. Lets breake vp Court, If Norfolke long should stay, In teares and passion, I should melt away.
O God! is shee a begg •… r, a forsaken Maide, that she hath neede of grace from forr •… ine princes? By Gods deare mother, O God p •… rdon swea •… e I, Me thinkes she is a faire and louely Prince, Her onely beautie (were she of mea •… e birth) Able to make the greatest 〈◊〉 , I the great Emperor of the 〈◊〉 Cham, That hath mor •… 〈◊〉 vnder his Commaund, Then spanish Philip's like to inherrit townes, To come and lay his Sc •… pter at her feet, And to intreate her to vouchsafe the grace To take him and his Kingdome to her mercy.

God morrow to the Patron of my woe. Nay why doth Iane, thus with a heauie eye, And a defected looke, salute the day? Sorrow doth ill become thy siluer brow, Sad griefe lyes dead, so long as thou liues fayre, In my Ianes ioy, I doe not care for care. Though sleepe doe sildome dwéll in men of care, Yet I did this night sleepe, and this night dream't, My Princely father great (Northumberland) Was marryed to a stately Bride: And then me thought, iust on his Bridall day, A poysoned draught did take his life away. The nights are teadious, and the daies are sad, And see you how the people stand in heapes, Each man sad, looking on his aposed obiect, As if a generall passion possest them? Their eyes doe seeme, as dropping as the Moone, As if prepared for a Tragedie. For neuer swarmes of people there doe tread, But to rob life, and to i •… ch the dead And shewe they wept. Our doomes are knowne, Our liues haue plaide their parte, Farwell my Iane. Great griefes speake louder When the least are dumb'd. EEx •… Patience my louely Iane: Patience has blancht thy soule, as white as snow, But who shall answere for thy death? this know, An innocent to die, what is it lesse, But to 〈◊〉 Angels 〈◊◊◊〉 , The guiltie dying, doe applaud the law, But when the innocent creature stoopes his neck to an vniust doome; vpon the Iudge they check.
